issues.legal_issue: A decree against a benamidar binds the beneficial owner who was not joined as a party when the benamidar or the benamidar’s heirs adequately represented the owner’s interest in the proceedings.
material_facts: The land stood in the name of a benamidar who acted for the beneficial owner, and the dispute with a third party proceeded through arbitration and court proceedings against the benamidar.
The beneficial owner participated in the arbitration process as the benamidar’s attorney and actively pursued objections to the award on the benamidar’s behalf.
After the benamidar died, the benamidar’s heirs adopted the objections and vigorously advanced the available challenges to the award on the beneficial owner’s behalf.
The beneficial owner’s application to join the proceedings was rejected, but the court observed that the decree would not bind him; whether he would be bound was not then in issue.
The decree was made in accordance with the award, and the beneficial owner later obstructed delivery of possession under it.
issues.conclusion: The beneficial owner was bound by the decree despite not being joined as a party, and the decree could be executed against him to require him to vacate the property.
issues.legal_principle: Under Gur Narayan v. Sheo Lal Singh, 46 Ind App 1 (AIR 1918 PC 140), a benamidar may represent the beneficial owner in litigation with a third party, and the result binds the owner unless it is shown that the benamidar could not or did not in fact represent the owner’s interest. Disclosure of the benami relationship and an unsuccessful application to join the owner do not, by themselves, end that representation. The Court found support in Prokash Chandra v. Mahima Ranjan and rejected the broad observations in Mata Prasad v. Ram Charan Sahu, ILR 36 All 446 (AIR 1914 All 173). The decree was executable against the beneficial owner under Order XXI, Rule 35 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

rule.if: award_enforcement_proceeding and benamidar_acted_for_beneficial_owner and (benamidar_or_heirs_adequately_represented_owner or not shown_representation_failed)

predicates.award_enforcement_proceeding: The dispute proceeded through enforcement of an award in court.
predicates.benamidar_acted_for_beneficial_owner: The person named in the property settlement acted on behalf of the beneficial owner.
predicates.benamidar_or_heirs_adequately_represente: The named person, and later that person’s heirs, advanced the beneficial owner’s interests and available challenges in the proceedings.
predicates.not shown_representation_failed: No showing established that the named person could not or did not represent the beneficial owner’s interests.

issues.definition: When an award-enforcement proceeding concerns a person who acted for a beneficial owner, and that person or their heirs adequately represented the owner or representation was not shown to have failed, the beneficial owner is bound by the decree.

issues.legal_issue: A new challenge to the High Court’s revisional jurisdiction should not be permitted for the first time on appeal when allowing it would cause grave injustice and the opposing party could otherwise obtain the same relief through a separate suit.
material_facts: The appellant challenged the High Court’s power to interfere under its revisional jurisdiction, but had not raised that contention in the High Court.
The award had been made years earlier, the decree had been entered, and the respondent had been deprived of the property for an extended period.

The Court considered that, if the High Court had dismissed the revision on jurisdictional grounds, the respondent would have brought a separate suit to establish the right to the property, and the appellant would have had no defence because the earlier decree bound him.
issues.conclusion: The appellant was not permitted to raise the new jurisdictional contention on appeal; the Court expressly left undecided whether the contention had merit.
issues.legal_principle: The Court declined to entertain a contention not raised in the High Court because doing so would, in the circumstances, cause grave miscarriage of justice. It did not decide the merits of the challenge under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.appellate_review_proceeding: A party sought appellate review of an order made in an execution-related revision proceeding.
predicates.new_jurisdictional_ground_not_raised_bel: The appellant raised a challenge to the reviewing court’s jurisdiction that had not been raised before that court.
predicates.allowing_ground_would_cause_grave_injust: The Court considered that allowing the new contention would cause grave miscarriage of justice in the circumstances.
predicates.respondent_could_obtain_same_relief_in_s: The respondent could have brought a separate suit for the property and the appellant would have had no defence to that claim.

issues.definition: In appellate review, a new jurisdictional ground not raised below is not permitted when allowing it would cause grave injustice and the opposing party could obtain the same relief in a separate suit.
